beats.label: SHAPED BY

cue.prompt: The system taught you how to move.

slides.title: BERLIN IS YELLOW
beats: 1980: Spiekermann tells the BVG its city looks like a mess. They say no.
1987: he gets 50 minutes — and insults every department head inside 15.
1989: the Wall falls. Two systems, one city, nobody can navigate.
1992: one drawing, several metres long. Berlin becomes yellow.
slides.note:
→ "This is a twelve-year cold pitch. That's the honest version of this story."

→ "1980, he tells the transit authority its city looks like a mess. They turn him down — 'unchangeable standards, a lack of responsibility and a lack of resources.'"

→ "1987 he finally gets fifty minutes in a room, and insults every department head inside fifteen. It backfires — but they remember him."

→ "Then history does the work. 1989 the Wall comes down, and a city split since 1949 has one transit network that nobody can read."

→ "1992 he unrolls a drawing several metres long that holds the whole system in one view."

⚑ He did NOT design the U-Bahn map. Dates above are verified — stick to them.

slides.text: Everything becomes yellow.
slides.note:
→ "One decision: everything becomes yellow. Buses, trams, signage — all of it."

→ "That's not a brand refresh. It's a cognitive system a citizen can navigate at speed."

→ "The city gets an identity that doesn't require explanation. Yellow becomes shorthand for movement."

· And the board buys it partly because it CUT COSTS — fewer buttons, fewer materials, fewer colours.

· This is my own line from the DDX writeup: branding at this scale behaves like electrical current. Invisible when it works, impossible to ignore when it's misaligned.

slides.text: Infrastructure works best when it disappears into use.
slides.note:
→ "Typography as nervous system, not ornament."

→ "The Deutsche Bahn typeface is recognizable with the logo removed. A mug with 'Bahn' on it in that face is unmistakable."

→ "Type isn't decoration. It carries identity through repetition and trust."

· I called it a neural signature — how a place senses itself. Proprioception for a city.

· Optional, only if the room is warm: I told him I liked his attitude and he said "What attitude? I'm German."

slides.text: Does it work? Nobody knows.
slides.note:
→ "Here's the turn, and it's the actual point."

→ "Eye magazine, 1995: his studio had almost no control over how the work got used. No pilot evaluation. He kept complaining that what the signs said and where they were placed were beyond his control."

→ "Asked whether the system worked, the answer was 'nobody knows.'"

→ "So he shaped the city — and the institution shaped him right back."

⚑ No ridership or legibility numbers. No MetaDesign co-founder names. Never repeat the Green Party claim.

slides.text: The constraint is the container.
slides.note:
→ "His closing point at DDX was deceptively deep: never put more than seven people on a project."

→ "Past that, human cognition reorganizes into subgroups. Communication fragments and the work slows."

→ "His metaphor: work is a gas. It expands. The constraint is the container."

· Tie it back — the shape of the org shapes the artifact. Berlin got legible because a small team with a hard constraint made one decision.

· This is the bridge to the next beat: the system shaped him, and he shaped it back.

beats.label: RESIST

slides.title: THE PEOPLE'S SIDEWALKS
beats: "We've tried cripples before, and they just don't work out."
Berkeley builds curb ramps. The disabled community says: wrong.
Flat ramps erase the edge blind pedestrians navigate by.
So they mapped 125 of them and drew the compromise themselves.
slides.note:
→ "Ed Roberts got polio at fourteen. Berkeley admitted him in 1962, and a dean's recorded reaction was 'we've tried cripples before, and they just don't work out.'"

→ "The only building that could hold his 800-pound iron lung was the campus hospital. He took it — on condition it be treated as a dorm, not a medical facility."

→ "More disabled students arrive. They name themselves the Rolling Quads, and they start using civil-rights language for something that had always been framed as charity."

→ "1969, after the People's Park riots, Berkeley renovates Telegraph Avenue and puts in wide flat curb ramps."

→ "The response is not gratitude. Flat ramps erase the edge blind pedestrians navigate by, and the diagonal angle pushes wheelchairs toward turning cars."

→ "And here's the best detail — the disabled community was split against itself. Wheelchair users and blind pedestrians wanted opposite things."

→ "So from 1970 to 1974 they map 125 curb-cut locations along Telegraph and Shattuck, and propose a steeper cut set outside the pedestrian crossing. A compromise they negotiated among themselves."

slides.text: Everyone with a stroller uses what they won.
slides.note:
→ "First planned wheelchair-accessible route in the United States, designed by disabled people."

→ "Sixteen years later the ADA makes it federal law. Today every stroller, suitcase and hand truck rides it."

→ "That's the loop closing: the system defined them as unable to move, they moved anyway, they redrew the environment — and the redrawn environment redefined everyone else's mobility."

→ "Adapt, resist, reshape — and then it inherits."

· Read as a sequence, not options. Berkeley ran all four.

beats.presenterNotes:
⏱ 6 min · this is the brief's "adapt, resist, reshape" promise

⚑ Roberts did NOT found the Center for Independent Living — say he led it or guided its growth · Berkeley did NOT invent the curb cut (Kalamazoo, 1940s, disabled veterans) · the defensible claim is first PLANNED accessible route, designed by disabled people

· Source: Bess Williamson, "The People's Sidewalks," Boom, Spring 2012

beats.label: RESPONSIBILITY

cue.prompt: For whose interests does the interface serve?

slides.title: REGENT / THE SEAGLIDER
beats: Brief: an interface for a captain who can fly.
Then the test pilot showed up. Call sign: Bob Dylan.
"That's not where I expect it to be."
We weren't designing interface. We were translating fluency.
slides.note:
→ "Regent builds a ground-effect craft that skims above the water."

→ "The client defined the operator as a mariner. One wheel, one throttle — a captain that can fly."

→ "But the operational scope was aviation-grade and the mental model was maritime. That gap was the entire design problem."

→ "Then a test pilot joins. Ex-Air Force, F-16s in service, 747s commercially, tens of thousands of hours. Call sign a folksinger's name — we called him Bob Dylan."

→ "He liked every concept. Every concept was wrong."

→ "Not messy, not unpolished — they didn't match the logic his body had spent decades building. He'd tell me what he couldn't see, not because it was missing from the UI but because it wasn't where his body expected it."

→ "The real user changed, and the entire prompt changed with it."

· Name the table: me, business development, product management, the CTO, program directors — all genuinely good people. Then the pilot arrived and reordered everything.

slides.title: SELF-CHECKOUT
beats: The chain protecting margins. The card companies extracting fees.
Age verification. Municipal regulation. Produce indexing.
slides.note:
→ "Self-checkout is the everyday version of the same table."

→ "The grocery chain protecting margins. The card companies extracting fees. Age verification. Municipal regulation. Produce vendors. And the machine itself, ever-ready to flag an unexpected item in the bagging area."

→ "What looks frictionless is a dense web of actors with motives, limits and influence."

slides.text: For whose interests does the interface serve?
slides.note:
→ "To design responsibly is to name those actors, question their power, and decide how — and whether — they belong at the table."

→ "It's one thing to design a beautiful interface in your tool of choice. It's another to negotiate with stakeholders. Both are valid, and both land in the interface — the place where the negotiation gets painted."

→ "Send me your answer on SIGNAL now. We're using them next."

slides.text: RIPTA is moving the bus hub out of Kennedy Plaza. Who was at that table?
slides.note:
→ "RIPTA's board voted in August to move the bus hub from Kennedy Plaza to the train station. Riders organized against it. The Kennedy Plaza Resilience Coalition has been fighting it since 2021."

→ "People in this room know this fight better than I do. So: who was at that table, and who wasn't?"

⚑ ASK, never assert. Do NOT state cost figures — they conflict (17M bond, 77M set aside, 200M estimates). Do NOT attribute motive to any named developer; that's reported opinion.
· Stage the sharpest RIPTA card. Let the room correct me — that's the point of asking.
